title: Dedicated capacity intake: transient spike handling, SLA bucketing, and GPU-class acceptance criteria
creator: Aisha K. Patel
description: Goal: define an operationally-safe, measurable triage flow for enterprise dedicated capacity requests where customers expect reserved throughput and strict SLA guarantees, but workloads include unpredictable transient spikes (e.g., RLHF bursts, weekend batch jobs, sudden API-driven campaigns). This ticket produces (1) an intake questionnaire extension that captures spike characteristics, (2) an SLA bucketing model that separates steady baseline vs burst reserve, (3) GPU-class acceptance criteria for each bucket, and (4) a recommended autoscaler profile and fallback ladder for Dedicated pools.
background_and_problem: Current intake forms and playbooks assume steady-state throughput and large, long-lived commitments. Several recent customers requested guaranteed tail-latency targets under spiky load; some early Dedicated pools saw preemption or cross-tenant degradation during unexpected bursts. Engineering has partial kernel scheduling mitigations, but we need product-level acceptance criteria to avoid over-promising and to standardize negotiation with enterprise teams.
acceptance_criteria: Published intake questionnaire v2 that adds fields: expected burst rate (peak QPS), burst duration distribution (p50/p95/p99), predictable seasonality windows, and RLHF-specific KV-cache characteristics
SLA bucketing doc describing: baseline reserved throughput (steady), burst credits pool (short-term), and emergency burst lanes with associated cost/latency tradeoffs
Clear GPU-class mapping table (A100-80GB, H100, L4-equivalent) with minimum acceptance thresholds for latency and throughput per model class
Autoscaler profile templates (conservative, balanced, aggressive) with example parameter sets and cost impact estimates
A runbook for sales/onboarding that lists gating questions, red-lines (non-negotiable constraints), and OSS/Enterprise template language for contracts
Sign-off from Eng (runtime team) and Solutions (SE) on feasibility and a small scope pilot plan with 2 customers
proposed_solution_summary: Introduce a two-tier reservation model: steady baseline (month-to-month committed GPU vCPU throughput) + burst credits (time-limited pool purchased or auto-borrowed with penalty). Intake captures spike telemetry; product recommends GPU class based on model profile + latency SLO. Autoscaling profiles provide deterministic warm-up paths (pre-warming KV cache, ramp-up windows) to reduce tail-latency risk.
tradeoffs_and_risks: Overly conservative GPU-class assignment increases customer cost; aggressive assignment risks SLA breaches and operational toil
Burst credits introduce billing complexity and potential disputes if telemetry is ambiguous
Pre-warming strategies reduce latency but increase idle cost unless we implement transient preemption or cheaper warm pools
implementation_notes: Work with ENG runtime to standardize a small set of 'burst-safe' model fingerprints (sequence length, kv-cache warmup time, token-generation p50/p95) that inform GPU-class recommendations. Build a lightweight intake UI change (Console) and a templated email for SEs. Pilot with two customers: one RLHF-heavy startup and one enterprise with nightly batch peaks.
